flawed_step: The proof would need Hall's condition: |N(S)| ≥ |S| for every S ⊆ A. The hypotheses don't give this. Counting edges from S gives |S| ≤ e(S, N(S)) ≤ 2|N(S)|, so only |N(S)| ≥ |S|/2. That bound is too weak for a matching that saturates A.
counterexample: Let A = {a1, a2}, B = {b1}, and the edges be a1–b1 and a2–b1. Both a1 and a2 have degree 1, so every vertex of A has degree at least 1. b1 has degree 2, so every vertex of B has degree at most 2. Every edge uses b1, so a matching has at most one edge. It can cover only one of a1 and a2, so no matching saturates A. (Hall's condition fails for S = A, since |N(A)| = 1 < 2.)
assessment_summary: The statement is false. The degree conditions only guarantee |N(S)| ≥ |S|/2 for S ⊆ A, not Hall's condition. A cherry graph, where two A-vertices share one B-vertex of degree 2, meets both conditions but has no matching that saturates A.
